author: zicokolter
text: @tdietterich Though to be honest, the question of "which kinds of distribution shifts can test-time adaptation adaptation handle" is still largely a mystery to me.

author: zicokolter
text: It's still a mystery, honestly, but one that appears consistently enough to prove extremely useful in practice, and hopefully can start to shed some light on why something as crazy as TENT might just actually work well after all. 19/N, N=19

author: zicokolter
text:
What on earth is happening here?  First, to be fully transparent, we don't really know.  But we have a conjecture.  And to explain it, I'll need to take you on a bit of detour, and define a function called the convex (Fenchel) conjugate. 12/N 

https://t.co/RlhiA9utqe https://t.co/GwGKToeKv4

author: zicokolter
text: But why softmax entropy?  It seem so arbitrary.  So I know, let's _meta-learn_ a different test-time adaptation objective, parameterized by some arbitrary neural network (a Transformer sounds good), to find the "right" test time loss that we should be optimizing. 7/N

author: zicokolter
text: Test-time adaptation is one strategy for accomplishing this, of which a classic example is the TENT method of Wang et al.  Basically, you take your unlabeled data, and minimize the entropy of the softmax logits of the classifier applied to these unlabeled data. 5/N

author: zicokolter
text: Most people probably know the basic setup of the setting we consider. You train on one distribution, but at test/deployment time, you face some form of distribution shift. You want to make your classifier to work well on the new distribution, using only _unlabeled_ data. 4/N

author: zicokolter
text: @BlackHC But regardless, the main relevant point to the general discussion I'm trying to have here is that I'm perfectly fine with _that_ mode of discussion (it would have been nice, IMO, to have simply discussed with us, but whatever).  It's the Twitter mode that I'm much less fond of.

author: zicokolter
text:
@BlackHC I guess you also felt the proof was "trivial", but I don't know, I don't really think your version is trivial either. 😅

Regardless, it did seem like we were talking past each other by the end, not really on technical points but on interpretations. 🤷‍♂️

author: zicokolter
text: @BlackHC Diving in a bit, I should also point out that we weren't disagreeing on the correctness of the proof or anything, but on the extent to which our paper "implied" anything about OOD data in general in theory, which we tried to take _great_ pains not to.

author: zicokolter
text: @BlackHC And to be fair, I didn't say anything critical about this.  I _still_ think your critique is largely misplaced (for all the reasons Vaishnavh details in the reply right after your rebuttal), but OpenReview _was_ absolutely a reasonable venue for such discussion.

author: zicokolter
text: @thejonullman I also think the "middle ground" is clear: good faith discussion with authors to try to ensure there are no misunderstandings, then try to reach consensus on points of disagreement.  If this cannot be achieved, then detailed rebuttals (on both sides).  Isn't that reasonable?

author: zicokolter
text: @shortstein Sure, but I mean, isn't in-person detailed discussion literally the ideal solution to this?  The exact venue exists for facilitating the right form of interaction.  We should be using it more?

author: zicokolter
text: @shortstein Isn't this better venue ... having discussions at a conference?

author: zicokolter
text: @MiroDudik Indeed, seems I was objectively wrong on that impression. :-)

author: zicokolter
text: @jhasomesh Some people found great value in them. Others had questions. That is fine. This is what the scientific process is for. I just think that the current interactions come across as _way_ more personal than those doing the criticizing maybe realize.

author: zicokolter
text: @jhasomesh As I think we discussed last we met (see, I promise I talk about this constantly 🤣) , I'm fully in agreement on tamping down improper incentives.  I just am also not  ready to concede that these papers _necessarily_ were rushed.

author: zicokolter
text: @mraginsky @abeirami @kamalikac But I _also_ think these kinds of responses tend to beg the question, and implicitly assume that the papers are unworthy. I genuinely am not attempting to address the scientific question of these particular cases here (well, I guess I am a bit for one of them).

author: zicokolter
text: @mraginsky @abeirami @kamalikac I think I mostly agree.  Approximately half of my academic discussions seem to venture into discussions on how we need to fix the status quo, and why our current efforts are not addressing the right problem.

author: zicokolter
text: @shortstein And in many cases in the past, I have found that rushed statements about a paper being "wrong" are often latered tempered, or at least qualified to speak to only a (perhaps small) portion of the paper. And the rush judgement produces _extremely_ negative impact on junior authors.

author: zicokolter
text: @shortstein I mean, I'm (hopefully obviously) not trying to claim here that scientific rigor _doesn't_ matter, certainly. I am all for thorough dissection of papers and their quality. I just think there are much better / more genuinely productive ways to have these discussions.

author: zicokolter
text: The "field" will be just fine, even in the unthinkable event that papers with some really interesting ideas also have a few honest mistakes, and win a few awards. 10/N, N=10.

author: zicokolter
text: Let's celebrate the papers and authors right now, look for the aspects that warrant excitement (and again, in some cases I think there there are zero merits to the criticism anyway). 9/N

author: zicokolter
text: All nuance and discussion, all the important aspects of the paper, any mistakes in the critiques, this is all lost. And even if authors engage, Twitter defaults to trust "the independent experts" more. It is an impossible situation for them. 7/N

author: zicokolter
text: I will accept that the original critiques are probably in good faith, but I think heavily misguided. Claims that this is about larger process fall flat ... the reviewers, ACs, SACs, award committees, whoever, they are not the ones with their names on the paper. 6/N

author: zicokolter
text: But we need to be honest about who bears 99% of the brunt of this very public and immediate criticism: the PhD student first authors. I can't *fathom* how stressful this must be for them. *I* have been stressed just thinking about it, and I have zero connection to the papers. 4/N

author: zicokolter
text: First off, my statements are independent of actual possible issues with the papers.  I think one of the criticisms likely has some merit but the authors would claim it is missing the main point of the work. The other seems baseless. That's all I'll say on that. 2/N

author: zicokolter
text: It's hard to say we _wouldn't_ do it again in hindsight, given that obviously it played a bit role in getting exposure for the paper.  We're leaving some in, but we decided not to keep, e.g., the "Note on paper length" for the Arxiv version. 15/

author: zicokolter
text: We genuinely thought this would mostly raise a chuckle from the reviewers, but it rubbed some people the wrong way.  And looking past, I can see how people took it as a bit passive-aggressive (though of course others got a kick out of it too). 14/

author: zicokolter
text: Now the second aspect, though, is the admittedly cheeky presentation.  The paper is so different from past papers we've written in the group that it just felt appropriate to lean a bit into the absurdity of such a simple concept. 13/

author: zicokolter
text: The paper is an extremely simple idea, and it's fine to have a short form paper for it, to convey these simple points.  I'm happy to debate anyone on this. 12/

author: zicokolter
text: The main text has the information needed to replicate the architecture.  And a summary of what we believe to be the critically important results from experiments.  The appendix has more detailed results.  This is how it should be. 11/

author: zicokolter
text: The short paper form, _including_ leaving several of the detailed results to the appendix, is something we still believe in adamantly, despite reviewer comments on this.  We won't be changing it. 10/

author: zicokolter
text: So speaking of the meme format, a few comments. But I should highlight that there are two aspects that I consider quite different: the short-format paper vs. the meme-ness (is that a word?). 9/

author: zicokolter
text: And as for the negative reactions, I don't deny that meme format played a role: e.g., the only real remaining objection of the negative reviewer that responded was that the "manuscript is not ready for a decent publication yet". 8/

author: zicokolter
text: More negative reactions seem basically split on whether the results are "obvious" or "wrong". But I think the overall reaction (which I admit was pretty unexpected) has been excitingly positive. 7/

author: zicokolter
text: FWIW, I also think that it's (probably not incorrectly) relatively hard to get such "reductionist" papers accepted.  Proposing something simple, that alone also has substantial drawbacks, always raises objections that you didn't compare precisely to X. 6/

author: zicokolter
text: It's observing that, stripped away of almost all cruft, and made comparable in architecture to modern Transformer networks, ConvNets still work really well.  I think it's extremely valuable to study architectures like this in their "minimal" form. 5/

author: zicokolter
text: First, I do think a main point here is still being obscured.  While it's absolutely awesome that an 80%+ ImageNet accuracy architecture fits into a tweet, the real goal of the paper isn't trying to propose anything particularly novel from an architecture standpoint. 4/

author: zicokolter
text: The paper didn't get into ICLR, FYI.  We disagree with the more critical reviewer comments, naturally, but such is life.  Some thoughts on the architecture/context, plus some later on the meme-ish paper format. 3/
